title: Study design
stem: An evening study-space QR invitation recruits 160 first-year volunteers. They report their sleep and complete a common quiz. **Which statement is most appropriate?**

options.A: A larger sample would remove the recruitment bias.
options.B: Volunteering makes the study a randomised experiment.
options.C: The study can identify associations, subject to recruitment limits.
options.D: Using the same quiz makes the sample representative.

reasons.A: More observations reduce chance variation, not systematic selection bias.
reasons.B: Random allocation of a treatment defines a randomised experiment.
reasons.C: Sleep is observed. Selection bias and confounding remain possible.
reasons.D: A common measurement does not change how students were recruited.

sources: Topic 1 pp. 25–38; Topic 8 pp. 12–22; Challenge 1 and 8; sample MCQ Q2, Q14; sample EA part (a).

title: Linking student records
stem: A researcher wants to link the sleep survey to individual university marks. The original consent covered only the survey. **Which action is most appropriate before linking the records?**

options.A: Remove names, then link records without checking consent.
options.B: Publish the linked records after replacing student numbers.
options.C: Assume a larger dataset makes privacy concerns negligible.
options.D: Check consent and ethics requirements, then limit and secure the data.

reasons.A: Removing names alone does not resolve consent or re-identification risks.
reasons.B: Replacing an identifier does not necessarily make linked records anonymous.
reasons.C: More data can increase the risk of identifying an individual.
reasons.D: Check the new use, minimise the linked data and protect access.

sources: Module 1, Topic 1: ethics and data linkage; current sample MCQ Q1. LO1.

title: Transforming variables
stem: The following summaries describe the 160 students. A new variable is defined in R. **What are its mean, SD and correlation with Score?**
stimulus:
```text
mean(Sleep)          7.0
sd(Sleep)            1.2
cor(Sleep, Score)    0.4114
```

```r
SleepIndex = 10 - 2 * students$Sleep
```

reasons.A: 10 − 2×7 = −4. SD is multiplied by 2 and correlation changes sign.
reasons.C: Reversing the direction of Sleep changes the correlation’s sign.

sources: Topics 3 and 5; Challenges 3.3 and 5.3; Exam Guide transformations; sample MCQ Q4.

title: Normal probabilities in R
stem: Assume $X\sim N(7,1.2^2)$ models nightly sleep. **Which R expression calculates $P(5.8<X<9.4)$?**

reasons.A: The third argument of pnorm is the SD, not the variance.
reasons.B: The subtraction is reversed, giving a negative number.
reasons.C: This adds the two tails outside the required interval.
reasons.D: Subtract the lower-tail area at 5.8 from the area at 9.4.

sources: Topic 4 pp. 10–25; Challenge 4; Revision Quiz 4 Q18/Q25/Q26; sample MCQ Q6.

title: Measurement error
stem: A tracker measures the **same fixed duration** 36 times under the same conditions. Each reading has a bias of +20 minutes and an independent chance error with mean 0 and SD 12 minutes. **For the average of the 36 readings, what are the bias and SE?**

reasons.A: Averaging reduces chance error. The common +20 minute bias remains.
reasons.B: The spread of the average is smaller than the spread of one reading.
reasons.C: Bias remains +20. The SE is 12 / sqrt(36) = 2 minutes.
reasons.D: The fixed bias remains. SE is divided by sqrt(36), not 36.

sources: Module 2, Topic 4: measurement error; Module 3, Topic 7: SE of a mean; current sample MCQ Q7. LO4 and LO6.

title: Conditional probability
stem: R gives the following counts. One student is chosen at random **from those sleeping below 7 hours**. What is the probability they report 2+ caffeinated drinks per day?
stimulus:
```r
table(students$SleepGroup,
      students$Caffeine)
```

| Sleep group | 0 | 1 | 2+ | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Below 7 h | 12 | 24 | 44 | 80 |
| At least 7 h | 28 | 32 | 20 | 80 |
| Total | 40 | 56 | 64 | 160 |

reasons.A: This conditions on 2+ drinks rather than short sleep.
reasons.B: The relevant group contains 80 students, of whom 44 report 2+ drinks.
reasons.C: This is the joint probability among all 160 students.
reasons.D: This is the marginal probability of 2+ drinks.

sources: Topic 6 conditional probability; Challenge 6 prosecutor fallacy; Revision Quiz 6 Q1/Q7/Q8; Week 13 recap p24.

title: Binomial probability in R
stem: A box model has a 0.4 chance of a 2+ drinks ticket. Five tickets are drawn independently with replacement. Let X count the 2+ tickets. **Which R expression gives the chance of at least two?**

reasons.A: At least two is the complement of zero or one.
reasons.B: This gives more than two, so it excludes X = 2.

sources: Module 3, Topic 6: Binomial model and pbinom; Challenge 6; current sample MCQ Q12 and Exam Guide. LO6.

title: Sampling distributions
stem: A population has mean sleep **7 hours** and SD **1.2 hours**. Independent observations are sampled with replacement. **What are the EV and SE of the sample mean when n increases from 25 to 100?**

reasons.B: A larger sample reduces the SE.
reasons.C: The EV of a sample mean remains the population mean.
reasons.D: $SE=1.2/\sqrt{100}=0.12$. Four times n gives half the SE.

sources: Topic 7 pp. 26–32,45,55; Challenge 7 and 8; Revision Quiz 7 Q6/Q10; Week 13 workshop Report 2 Q2.

title: Bootstrapping the mean
stem: The observed survey has 160 complete Sleep values. We want a bootstrap distribution of the mean. **Which expression should replace RESAMPLE?**

reasons.A: Without replacement, every value appears once. Each mean is unchanged.
reasons.B: Each bootstrap sample has the original size and resamples the observed values with replacement.
reasons.C: This simulates from a Normal model rather than resampling the observed data.
reasons.D: 10,000 is the number of replicates. Each resample should still contain 160 values.

sources: Module 3, Topic 8: bootstrapping procedure, lecture pp. 48–52. LO6.

title: Using a confidence interval
stem: Sixteen students are measured before and after a phone-free fortnight. Let $D=\text{After}-\text{Before}$. Assume independent students and approximately Normal differences. **For the new two-sided test $H_0:\mu_D=0.75$ at 5%, which conclusion is correct?**
stimulus:
```r
t.test(D, mu = 0)
```

```text
t = 2, df = 15, p-value = 0.06395
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.03286  1.03286
sample mean: 0.5
```

options.A: Reject: the sample mean differs from 0.75.
options.B: Retain: 0.75 lies inside the 95% confidence interval.
options.D: Accept: there is a 95% probability the mean lies in this interval.

reasons.A: A sample estimate can differ from the null through chance variation.
reasons.B: A matching two-sided 5% test retains null values inside the 95% CI.
reasons.C: The printed p-value tests μD = 0. The new p-value is 0.3332.
reasons.D: The parameter is fixed. 95% refers to the CI method’s long-run coverage.

sources: Topic 10; Revision Quiz 10 Q1; sample MCQ Q17; Week 13 workshop Report 2 whiteboard task.

title: Linear regression
stem: A regression of Score on Sleep gives the following output and residual plot. **Which statement is most appropriate?**
stimulus: ```r fit = lm(Score ~ Sleep, data = students) summary(fit) ``` ```text Slope = 3.000 SE = 0.529 t = 5.674 p = 6.485e-08 ```

options.A: The changing residual spread raises concern about the usual slope inference.
options.B: The small p-value establishes constant residual variance.
options.C: The positive slope shows that more sleep caused higher scores.
options.D: A straight residual QQ plot would establish all model assumptions.

reasons.A: Increasing spread suggests heteroscedasticity. The usual test needs caution.
reasons.B: The slope test does not check the constant-variance condition.
reasons.C: Sleep was observed. Confounding remains possible.
reasons.D: A QQ plot checks Normality, not every LINE condition.

sources: Topic 5 pp. 39–50; Topic 11 pp. 47–53; Challenge 5 residual audit; sample MCQ Q8/Q10/Q20.

title: Choosing the chi-squared test
stem: We want to test whether **sleep group and caffeine category are associated**. Which row gives the test, expected count for **Below 7 h / 2+ drinks** and degrees of freedom?
stimulus:
| Sleep group | 0 | 1 | 2+ | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Below 7 h | 12 | 24 | 44 | 80 |
| At least 7 h | 28 | 32 | 20 | 80 |
| Total | 40 | 56 | 64 | 160 |

Here `tab` is the 2 × 3 table without its totals.

reasons.A: Equal-proportion GOF concerns one variable, not the association of two.
reasons.B: 44 is observed. Expected counts are calculated under independence.
reasons.D: $rc-1$ is not the df formula for an independence test.

sources: Topic 11 pp. 6–7,23–32; Challenge 11; Revision Quiz 11 Q8/Q11/Q19; sample EA Source 3.

title: Goodness of fit
stem: A model assigns equal population proportions to the three caffeine categories. Assume independent records and adequate expected counts. **What does this output support at the 5% level?**

options.A: Reject, because the three observed counts differ.
options.B: Retain, which establishes equal population proportions.
options.C: The probability that the equal-proportions model is true is 0.06081.
options.D: Retain, with insufficient evidence against equal population proportions.

reasons.A: Unequal counts can arise through chance even when the model holds.
reasons.B: Retaining a model does not prove it.
reasons.C: The p-value assumes the null model. It does not give its probability.
reasons.D: p > 0.05, so the data do not provide sufficient evidence against the model at this level.

sources: Module 4, Topic 11: chi-squared goodness of fit; Challenge 11; current sample MCQ Q18, Q29–30. LO7 and LO8.
